tei:titleStmt.tei:title: [Gebet] An den letzten Tagen des Laubhüttenfestes
[A prayer] on the last days of Sukkot, by Fanny Neuda (1855)

tei:div.tei:head: [Gebet] An den letzten Tagen des Laubhüttenfestes

tei:lg.tei:l: Today we bring the Feast of Tabernacles to a close, and my heart lifts up to You, O All-Merciful One, to thank You for every joyful, festive feeling You have allowed me to experience, and for every joyful, festive delight You have let me share in.

We have sat in huts, as you commanded, and have enjoyed our feasts there undisturbed and in joy; and with devout and festive hearts, as we raised our cups in celebration, we have hallowed and praised your name. We now leave these huts and move into our permanent dwellings with all their comforts and conveniences. May you also spread the shelter of your peace over us; may you never let us forget that you alone are the support and pillar of our home, the protection and shield of our lives, that it is you who bless the fields and meadows, the threshing floor and the winepress, that You adorn our earthly life with the gifts of Your grace and open the gates of Your heavenly dwellings to us when the tent of our body and life here on earth collapses around us.

Our life is indeed a booth of leaves, with green leaves of hope forming the roof, the walls adorned with ornaments and decorations, and the table set with inviting, tempting delights. We may well celebrate joyful feasts within it and look out happily upon the friendly natural world, but all too often the sky grows dark, and in the midst of our merry feasts, in the midst of our festive joys, the cold shivers of misfortune suddenly pierce us, and heavy drops of bitter suffering and sorrow fall upon us; the harsh north wind cuts through the cheerful, fresh foliage of our hopes, stripping away leaves and wreaking destruction, and the storm shakes and rattles the walls and pillars of our happiness; one flower of joy after another falls, stripped of its petals, at our feet; one adornment of life after another is lost; deep sorrow pierces our soul, and we believe ourselves abandoned to the injustice of fate. Then our only consolation is that our whole life is but a festival in a hut, lasting only a few days. Soon this earthly dwelling will crumble around us, our mortal shell will fall away, and our soul will return to the imperishable abodes of heaven; left behind are all earthly joys, which are for the most part so unsatisfying, which always leave so much still to hope for and desire; left behind are all earthly hardships, all earthly sorrows and sufferings; but with us we take all our deeds and works, all acts of love we have performed here, all the sacrifices we have made for what is good and noble, all the tears that grateful hearts shed for us. They form the adornment and splendor of our heavenly abodes, which never fades and never passes away. There our hopes ripen into glorious fruit; there our merits blossom into their crowns; there all our sufferings are transformed into endless joys.

Let us remember all this, O God, so that it may serve as a lesson and a source of salvation for us on our earthly journey; so that we may never allow ourselves to be crushed by the heavy hand of misfortune; so that we may not become arrogant in the splendor and radiance of good fortune; so that we may not forsake the glories of eternal being for the adornments of fleeting huts; and so that our walk may always be a pure, holy, and pleasing to You. אָמֵן Amen.

tei:note.tei:p: From the Kriyat Shema al ha-Mita. Cf. Jerusalem Talmud Berakhot 35b:1
A reference to Qohelet (Ecclesiastes), traditionally read on the Shabbat of Sukkot
